paragraphs: Black Friday is a big sales day in November. But most shoppers in Ireland do not believe the low prices. A new survey shows this.
Only 23% of people believe the big discounts. In 2022, more people believed them. Most people will check the prices before they buy.
People also plan to spend less money. They expect to spend €307 on average. In 2024 it was €431. Many people say life is too expensive now.
More than half of people will only shop online. The consumer group CCPC says people should buy from shops in the EU. Then they can change their mind and get their money back.
sentZh: 黑色星期五是十一月的大型特賣日。
但愛爾蘭大多數購物者不相信那些低價。
一項新調查顯示了這一點。
只有23%的人相信大幅折扣。
在2022年，相信的人比較多。
大多數人在購買前會先查看價格。
人們也打算少花一點錢。
他們預計平均花費307歐元。
許多人說現在生活太貴了。
超過一半的人只會在網路上購物。
消費者機構CCPC說，人們應該向歐盟境內的商店購買。
這樣他們就可以改變主意並拿回退款。

paragraphs: Most Irish shoppers do not trust Black Friday discounts, a new survey has found. Only 23% believe that shops really offer big savings. This is the lowest level since the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) started asking in 2022.
Almost three in four people say the discounts cannot be trusted. Eight in ten would check the offers before spending money.
Shoppers also plan to spend less this year. The average person expects to spend €307, down from €431 in 2024. Almost half say the cost of living makes them less likely to shop in the sales.
More than half of people plan to shop only online. Nearly one in five admit they have shopped online after drinking alcohol, and half regret something they bought quickly in a sale.
The CCPC says shops must win back people's trust. It advises shoppers to buy from sellers in the EU, because they can change their mind within 14 days and get a full refund.
sentZh: 一項新調查發現，大多數愛爾蘭購物者不信任黑色星期五的折扣。
只有23%的人相信商店真的提供大幅優惠。
這是競爭與消費者保護委員會（CCPC）自2022年開始調查以來的最低水準。
將近四分之三的人說這些折扣不可信。
十人中有八人會在花錢前先查證優惠。
購物者今年也打算少花一些錢。
一般人預計花費307歐元，低於2024年的431歐元。
將近一半的人說，生活成本讓他們較不可能在特賣期間購物。
超過一半的人打算只在網路上購物。
將近五分之一的人承認曾在喝酒後上網購物，一半的人後悔在特賣時衝動買下的東西。
CCPC說，商店必須贏回人們的信任。
它建議購物者向歐盟境內的賣家購買，因為他們可以在14天內改變主意並獲得全額退款。

paragraphs: The vast majority of Irish consumers are sceptical about Black Friday deals, according to a new survey by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC). Just 23% of shoppers believe retailers' promises of big discounts, the lowest level since the CCPC began tracking attitudes in 2022.
Some 73% said the discounts were not trustworthy, up from 61% four years ago, while 80% said they would research offers before spending.

Spending plans have also fallen. The 1,028 people surveyed expect to spend an average of €307, down from €431 in 2024, and 47% said the rising cost of living made them less likely to shop in the sales.

More than half intend to shop exclusively online. Almost one in five admitted they had shopped online while under the influence of alcohol or drugs, and half regretted an impulse purchase made during a sale.

CCPC communications director Aoibhín de Búrca said retailers must work to win back consumer trust. She urged shoppers to buy from EU-based sellers, which gives them 14 days to change their minds and receive a full refund.

paragraphs: Irish consumers have grown deeply sceptical of Black Friday bargains, a new survey by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) suggests. A mere 23% of shoppers take retailers' promises of hefty discounts at face value, the lowest share since the watchdog began monitoring sentiment in 2022.
Fully 73% deem the discounts untrustworthy, up from 61% four years ago, and 80% intend to scrutinise offers before parting with their money.

Budgets are being reined in, too. The 1,028 respondents anticipate spending an average of €307, a steep drop from €431 in 2024, while 47% say the soaring cost of living has dampened their appetite for the sales.

Over half plan to shop exclusively online. Strikingly, almost one in five confessed to having shopped online while under the influence of alcohol or drugs, and half rued an impulse buy made in the heat of a sale.

Aoibhín de Búrca, the CCPC's communications director, said traders now face the task of winning back consumer confidence. She advised shoppers to favour EU-based sellers, whose customers are entitled to a 14-day cooling-off period and a full refund.

paragraphs: The overwhelming majority of Irish consumers express scepticism regarding Black Friday promotions, according to a recent survey conducted by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC). Only 23% of respondents consider retailers' claims of substantial discounts to be credible, the lowest proportion since monitoring commenced in 2022.
Furthermore, 73% regard such discounts as untrustworthy, an increase from 61% in 2022, while 80% indicated that they would investigate offers prior to making a purchase.

Anticipated expenditure has also declined considerably. The 1,028 participants expect to spend an average of €307, compared with €431 in 2024, and 47% reported that the escalating cost of living has reduced their likelihood of participating in the sales.

More than half intend to shop exclusively online. Notably, almost one in five acknowledged having made online purchases while under the influence of alcohol or drugs, and half expressed regret over an impulsive purchase made during a sale.

Aoibhín de Búrca, communications director at the CCPC, stated that retailers must endeavour to restore consumer confidence. She recommended purchasing from EU-based sellers, since consumers are consequently entitled to a 14-day period in which to change their minds and obtain a full refund.
